title: Supervision 8 essay
description: Discuss the relative importance of respiratory system and kidneys in regulating plasma pH.
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 8. Write it here, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Planning. Plan your essay before you start writing, on paper if you like.
  • Equations. Type simple ones into your text, as you’d write them by hand (× is among the special characters, under Ω). For one with a fraction, use the formula tool, Σ. Say what each equation means, and then use it.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your work.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Saving. Your work is saved in this browser as you type, so you can stop and come back to it. It stays here until you submit it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your work and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: The lungs and the kidneys
questions.text:
Discuss the relative importance of respiratory system and kidneys in regulating plasma pH.

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Support your argument with mechanisms, evidence and numbers from the lectures.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it before the supervision to look back over what you wrote. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers.

What the title asks. A judgement: which matters more, by what criteria, and when. It needs the respiratory lectures (the control of breathing, the chemoreceptors, CO2 transport) as well as the renal ones, and the disorders of acid–base balance are the evidence. An essay that describes the two systems in turn and concludes that “both are important” hasn’t answered it.

  • The framework. pH 7.4 ([H+] 40 nM), survivable over about 7.0–7.8; pH = 6.1 + log10([HCO3−]/(0.03 × PCO2)); the ratio of 20 matters, not either value alone. The bicarbonate buffer is powerful, despite a pK of 6.1, because the system is open and both members are regulated: CO2 by the lungs and HCO3− by the kidneys. Other buffers: phosphate, plasma proteins, haemoglobin and intracellular proteins.
  • The lungs. They excrete 12–15 mol of CO2 (volatile acid) a day, by far the largest acid load. Central chemoreceptors (the pH of the CSF, so PCO2) and peripheral ones (PO2, PCO2 and pH) adjust ventilation within minutes. They make physiological buffering possible (the CO2 formed when HCO3− buffers an acid is blown off) and compensate for metabolic disturbances: in ketoacidosis the PCO2 may fall by about 1.2 mmHg per mM fall in HCO3−. But compensation is partial, limited (the PCO2 can’t fall far, and hypoventilation to compensate an alkalosis is limited by hypoxia), and can’t restore HCO3−.
  • The kidneys. They reabsorb the filtered HCO3− (about 4300 mmol a day; most in the proximal tubule, by Na+/H+ exchange and carbonic anhydrase), make new HCO3− from glutamine (excreting NH4+) to replace what the daily 70 mmol or so of non-volatile acid uses up, excrete titratable acid (mainly H2PO4−; urine pH can’t fall below about 4.5, so free H+ can’t be the route), and secrete HCO3− in alkalosis (type B intercalated cells). They’re slow (days), but they correct, and compensate for respiratory disturbances (chronic respiratory acidosis; altitude, where HCO3− falls by about 4 mM per 10 mmHg fall in PCO2).
  • The liver belongs in a good answer: the urea cycle removes NH4+ and HCO3− together; in acidosis it makes more glutamine and less urea, giving the kidneys the substrate for new HCO3−. And the controversy in the handout: whether the kidneys excrete non-volatile acid (the older view) or mainly make new HCO3− while the acid leaves as CO2 through the lungs (the view in the lectures, supported by how little titratable acid the urine holds).
  • The evidence: disorders. Respiratory failure (an acute respiratory acidosis, then renal compensation); renal failure (a metabolic acidosis on a normal diet); ketoacidosis (respiratory compensation at once, renal correction later, if it can keep up); altitude; vomiting (a metabolic alkalosis, with hypoventilation); hypokalaemia and primary aldosteronism (a metabolic alkalosis from the kidney).
  • The judgement. It depends on the timescale and on the source of the disturbance: the lungs dominate minute to minute and handle much the largest load; the kidneys alone can restore HCO3−, and so the long-term balance. Either can compensate for the other, but neither can replace it.

What makes an essay stand out. Explicit criteria (speed, capacity, completeness, what each handles). Evidence from disorders, with numbers. The liver and the acid-removal controversy, used to sharpen the argument. And a conclusion that commits to a position and qualifies it.
